summary:
H.R. 3334, the “Sanctioning Tyrannical and Oppressive People within the Chinese Communist Party Act” (STOP CCP Act), mandates the President, not later than 30 days after enactment, to impose property-blocking and visa ineligibility sanctions under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.) and the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.) on four categories of persons: (1) members and alternate members of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) whom the President determines engage in sanctionable conduct; (2) members of any successor organization in the event of dissolution, if the President determines they engage in such conduct; (3) adult family members (including spouses and spouses’ adult family members) of persons described in (1) or (2); and (4) Chinese state-owned enterprises the President determines illegally manufacture or distribute fentanyl, or knowingly or intentionally manufacture or distribute fentanyl precursor chemicals for illegal production or distribution.

Sanctionable conduct, set out in section 4(b), requires a significant role in developing or implementing government policies or laws that the President determines appear designed to: violate Hong Kong’s autonomy; harass, intimidate, or increase aggression toward the people of Taiwan; contribute to political oppression or human rights violations against individuals or groups within the People’s Republic of China, including Uyghur Muslims; or willfully and knowingly engage in malicious activities, including online disinformation and propaganda, to interfere with U.S. elections.

Sanctions described in section 4(c) consist of: blocking all property and interests in property within U.S. jurisdiction; and rendering covered aliens inadmissible, ineligible for visas or parole, and revoking existing visas or entry documentation, effective immediately and canceling other valid visas, pursuant to section 221(i) of the INA (8 U.S.C. 1201(i)). Exceptions protect compliance with the United Nations Headquarters Agreement and authorized U.S. intelligence, law enforcement, and national security activities. Section 4(j) expressly excludes authority to impose sanctions on the importation of goods.

The President may waive sanctions for renewable 60-day periods under section 4(g), upon certification to specified congressional committees at least 15 days in advance that the waiver is vital to U.S. national security. Section 4(i) sunsets all waiver and license authorities two years after enactment. Termination of sanctions under section 4(h) requires the President to certify to Congress, and publicly post, that the PRC and CCP have ceased the specified actions (genocide against Uyghurs, oppression of Tibetans, threats and aggression toward Taiwan, undermining Hong Kong’s autonomy, and theft of U.S. intellectual property) or that a sanctioned individual has renounced CCP membership and remediated the conduct, or a sanctioned state-owned enterprise has ceased illicit fentanyl-related activities. The bill contains no authorization of appropriations; it relies on existing IEEPA authorities and imposes penalties from section 206 of IEEPA (50 U.S.C. 1705).
